newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Uzbekistan to set up joint commission.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Uzbekistan to set up joint commission.

text.p: The United States announced on Thursday it was setting up a joint commission to develop political and economic ties with Uzbekistan, a country of strategic location but a much-criticised human rights record.

The State Department said the U.S.-Uzbek commission would be inaugurated in the autumn of this year and would seek to push forward political, military, trade, investment and energy cooperation with the former Soviet Central Asian state.

The decision was taken during talks on Wednesday between Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and her deputy Strobe Talbott and Uzbek Foreign Minister Abdulaziz Komilov, spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
The United States already has joint commissions of various formats with Russia, Ukraine, Egypt, South Africa and Mexico -- all countries with which it enjoys much closer ties than with Uzbekistan.

But Burns said: "We have a promising relationship with Uzbekistan. It has certainly improved since the beginning of our relationship back in 1992 and 1993 ... This is a sign that we do want to improve our relationship with Uzbekistan."
Tashkent has been criticised by human rights groups and by the State Department itself for failure to tolerate serious political opposition.
President Islam Karimov, the country's former Communist Party boss, is anxious to boost ties with the United States and has spoken recently of the need to improve the rights situation in his country.
Burns said Albright and Talbott had underscored the need to strengthen human rights in Uzbekistan, promote economic reforms and improve the climate for foreign investment.
But he indicated that strategic and economic factors had weighed more heavily.

"If you look at the map and look at the natural resources, look at the proximity of Uzbekistan to Afghanistan, for instance -- Uzbekistan is one of the key countries in the Central Asian and Caucasus region in geopolitical terms," he said.
"Commercially, it's a very important country for the United States. And in terms of the conflict in Afghanistan, exceedingly important," he said.

Uzbekistan's importance was underscored during heavy fighting last month across the border in Afghanistan between the purist Islamic Taleban movement which holds much of the country and an ethnic Uzbek faction based in the north.

"During the course of the meetings with the Uzbek delegation, the United States expressed very clearly our support for the independence and sovereignty and integrity of Uzbekistan in its part of the world," Burns said.
